issues.legal_issue: A property-valuation scheme that removes a pre-decisional opportunity to object and provides only an ineffective, institutionally interested review fails the requirements of procedural fairness and equality.
material_facts: The amendment removed the process for publishing a draft valuation list and hearing objections before the valuation was finalized.
The valuation became conclusive subject only to a later review, which required payment or deposit of the assessed amount before an application could be entertained.
The review body included municipal representatives and a valuation-board officer, and its decision had to be unanimous; disagreement returned the matter to the Board.
The review body's powers were restricted, and ordinary civil-court proceedings were barred.
issues.conclusion: The review process was illusory and did not provide an effective hearing; the amended scheme violated Article 14 and was unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires a fair, non-arbitrary procedure when a decision imposes civil consequences. Under audi alteram partem, an affected person ordinarily must have a genuine opportunity to be heard before the decision; a later hearing may suffice only where it amounts to a full review on the merits. A remedy must be effective, and decision-makers must not be judges of their own cause. The Court relied on Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India (1981) 1 SCC 664; Calcutta Gujarati Education Society v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation (2003) 10 SCC 533; Rajesh Kumar v. D.C.I.T. (2007) 2 SCC 181; C.B. Gautam v. Union of India (1993) 1 SCC 78; Tulsiram Patel (1985) and Chief Security Officer v. Singasan Rabi Das (1991) 1 SCC 729, among other authorities.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_property_valuation_scheme and no_predecision_objection_opportunity and postdecision_review_was_limited and review_body_lacked_independence and effective_court_remedy_was_unavailable

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_val: The proceeding challenged the constitutionality of a scheme for valuing property for municipal taxation.
predicates.no_predecision_objection_opportunity: The scheme finalized property valuations without first giving affected persons an opportunity to object and be heard.
predicates.postdecision_review_was_limited: The scheme provided only a later review whose powers were restricted and whose decision was subject to constraints that could prevent full redress.
predicates.review_body_lacked_independence: The review body included representatives or officers connected to the authorities responsible for the valuation and taxation.
predicates.effective_court_remedy_was_unavailable: The scheme barred ordinary civil-court proceedings and left affected persons without an effective alternative remedy.

issues.definition: When a property-valuation challenge concerns a scheme with no pre-decision objection opportunity, only limited later review, a non-independent review body, and no effective court remedy, the scheme is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Property valuations based on an unscientific process conducted by untrained personnel under a delegation that leaves the responsible valuation authority without control are arbitrary and violate equality.
material_facts: The Board relied on data gathered through door-to-door surveys by casual municipal employees whose training and qualifications were not established.
The Board had delegated the survey work to the Municipality and had no demonstrated control over the employees or supervision of their work.
The valuations were not shown to rest on an expert or scientific method, and the valuation demands varied extremely across holdings.
The governing municipal legislation identified factors relevant to determining annual valuation.
issues.conclusion: The valuation method used was arbitrary and unconstitutional under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary state action. Valuation is an expert exercise that must use a rational, non-haphazard method and relevant valuation factors; a statutory authority cannot evade its responsibility through an uncontrolled delegation. The Court relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, AIR 1978 SC 597; Dr. Balbir Singh v. M.C.D. (1985) 1 SCC 167; Krishna Mohan (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi (2003) 7 SCC 151; and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685, and considered the valuation requirements under section 106 of the West Bengal Municipal Act, 1993 and section 9 of the West Bengal Central Valuation Board Act, 1978.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_valuation_method and valuation_data_was_collected_by_untrained_workers and responsible_authority_lacked_control_over_survey and no_scientific_expert_basis_was_shown and valuation_demands_varied_extremely

predicates.challenge_to_property_valuation_method: The proceeding challenged the method used to determine property valuations for municipal taxation.
predicates.valuation_data_was_collected_by_untraine: The municipal authority used casual workers whose relevant training and qualifications were not established to collect property data.
predicates.responsible_authority_lacked_control_ove: The authority responsible for valuation delegated survey work and did not demonstrate control or supervision over the people carrying it out.
predicates.no_scientific_expert_basis_was_shown: The valuation authority did not establish that its valuations rested on an expert, scientific, or otherwise rational method.
predicates.valuation_demands_varied_extremely: The resulting valuation demands differed extremely across the properties assessed.

issues.definition: When a property-valuation method relies on data collected by untrained workers without control by the responsible authority, lacks a demonstrated scientific or expert basis, and produces extremely varied demands, the method is arbitrary and unconstitutional.
